newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Doubts cast on reports of IRA meeting.
newsitem.headline: Doubts cast on reports of IRA meeting.

text.p: Irish officials and police cast doubt on Saturday about reports of an IRA guerrilla convention to review strategy.
They said it was possible that small groups of Irish Republican Army activists might be meeting but dismissed as implausible reports of 100 or more activists gathering in secret on Irish soil.
"We are totally unaware of any such meeting," said one government official.
Membership of the IRA is illegal in both the Irish Republic and the British province of Northern Ireland.

Television reports said the IRA had called a "Special Army Convention", said to be the guerrillas' top decision-making body, in Knock, a town in the west known mainly as a centre of Roman Catholic pilgrimage.
Police said they had no knowledge of any such meeting or of any gathering by known IRA activists or supporters.

According to the media reports, top members of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, were on their way or had been invited to Knock to discuss the next phase of IRA struggle against British rule in Northern Ireland.
Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams said in Belfast that the reports were bizarre and lacked credibility. He added that he would usually be aware of such a meeting.

The army convention has met only twice in the past 27 years, Irish historians say, at key phases in its campaign to force a British withdrawal from the province, whose 60 per cent Protestant majority wants to remain British.

The IRA ended a 17-month ceasefire in February with a string of attacks in Britain. The guerrilla group bombed the British army headquarters in Northern Ireland on October 7 in its first attack in the province since the ceasefire.
Michael Rogan, a 32-year-old kitchen designer, appeared in a Belfast court on Saturday and was charged with conspiracy in connection with the attack on army headquarters.
The British and Irish governments say Sinn Fein will be excluded from multi-party peace talks under way in Belfast until the IRA calls a new ceasefire.
But the IRA and Sinn Fein say the talks will attempt to disarm the guerrillas and reject any preconditions for the negotiations.
